12:4.text: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;

provenance.other: Hebrews 6:19 is a verse made almost entirely of KJV singletons. “anchor of the soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “sure and stedfast” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “within the veil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. All three are the same verse, and Ether 12 has all three.
provenance.significance: This is the structural key to the chapter, and it is missed if the verse is read only for its anchor image. Hebrews 6:19 says three things in sequence: hope is an anchor of the soul, it is sure and stedfast, and it enters within the veil. Ether 12:4 takes the first two — “hope … maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast” — and then holds the third in reserve for fifteen verses, until 12:19-21, where those whose faith is exceeding strong “could not be kept from within the veil” and the brother of Jared “could no longer be kept without the veil.” Moroni has distributed one KJV verse across the two halves of his discourse, and the veil that closes the argument is the veil the anchor of the opening sentence was already entering. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the reader who recovers Hebrews 6:19 finds that Moroni's veil was promised at the start.

12:4.note: “Whoso believeth in God, might with surety hope for a better world … which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast.” The KJV's one anchor-of-the-soul verse supplies the image, the plural “souls of men” for its singular “soul”, and the doublet “sure and stedfast” intact. Moroni's one substantive change is doctrinal rather than verbal: Hebrews says hope is the anchor, and Moroni adds a derivation, “which hope cometh of faith”, subordinating hope to the faith that is his subject. The link falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six; what carries it is three singletons from one verse, not length.

12:4.text: But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.

provenance.other: “better country” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The comparative-plus-place construction for the object of hope is Hebrews', not the Old Testament's.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:16 is the hinge of the faith chapter Moroni is about to recite: the patriarchs' faith is redescribed as desire for a better country which God has prepared. Ether 12:4's “hope for a better world” takes the construction, and the preparation motif Hebrews attaches to it (“he hath prepared for them a city”) then governs the end of Moroni's discourse, where the object of hope is four times “the place which thou hast prepared” (12:32, 12:34, 12:37). So the chapter's opening hope and its closing inheritance are held together by one verse of Hebrews 11 that Moroni never quotes outright.

12:4.note: “Might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God.” The KJV has exactly one comparative country-of-hope, and it is in the chapter Ether 12 is built on. Moroni substitutes “world” for “country” and glosses it with a location at God's right hand — a substitution rather than an independent coinage, since nothing else in the KJV licenses hoping for a better anything.

12:4.text: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

provenance.other: “always abounding” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Paul's phrase is “always abounding in the work of the Lord”, singular; Ether 12:4 has “always abounding in good works”, plural.
provenance.significance: Ether 12:4 fuses two exhortation-endings that are not related in the Bible. “Sure and steadfast” is Hebrews 6:19's; “steadfast … always abounding” is 1 Corinthians 15:58's; the word steadfast is the seam, and it belongs to both. The result is a sentence in which Paul's resurrection peroration and Hebrews' anchor of hope are welded at their one shared adjective. This is the pattern of the whole chapter — Moroni composes out of Hebrews and the Corinthian letters simultaneously — and 12:4 is where it is easiest to see.

12:4.note: “Which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.” The second half of the clause is 1 Corinthians 15:58's, in Paul's order: steadfast, then always abounding. Moroni's “good works” for Paul's “work of the Lord” is the ordinary Book of Mormon substitution, and the sequence steadfast → always abounding is what makes the borrowing visible rather than the individual words.

12:6.text: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

provenance.other: “things hoped for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “things not seen” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hebrews 11:1 and Hebrews 11:7, both in the same chapter. Both of Moroni's phrases are therefore Hebrews 11's, and they are in Hebrews 11:1's order.
provenance.significance: Moroni's version drops precisely the two abstract nouns — substance, evidence — and keeps the two phrases they govern, which is the reading the rest of the chapter needs: not a definition of what faith IS but a rule about what may be seen. The verse that follows makes the excision do work: “dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.” Hebrews 11:1 is a definition; Ether 12:6 is a procedure derived from it. The same verse is quoted at Alma 32:21 with a different excision (“ye hope for things which is not seen, which are true”) and read backwards at Ether 3:19, where the brother of Jared's sight ends his faith — three uses of one verse, none of them the same use.

12:6.note: “I would shew unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen.” This is the chapter's programmatic sentence and it is Hebrews 11:1 with the copular nouns removed: faith is [the substance of] things which are hoped for and [the evidence of things] not seen. The 1830 “shew” for the current “show” preserves the KJV spelling and is worth noting under CONVENTIONS §8; it is not itself evidence of this link, but it is evidence that the passage was composed in KJV English. Everything from 12:7 to 12:22 is the working-out of this verse, and Hebrews 11 is the model for that working-out as well.

12:6.text: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:

provenance.other: “trial of your faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. James 1:3 has the same idea in different English — “the trying of your faith worketh patience” — which is the comparison that shows how specific Moroni's wording is: he has Peter's noun, not James's gerund.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 1:7 is about a trial that vindicates faith at the appearing of Jesus Christ; Moroni turns it into an epistemic rule — no witness until after the trial. The transposition is the interesting part. Peter's trial is suffering; Moroni's is the period of not-seeing that 12:6 has just defined faith as. Recovering Peter's context supplies what Moroni's sentence leaves out, namely that the withheld witness is finally given, and given at an appearing.

12:6.note: “Ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.” Four words shared with the KJV's one occurrence of the phrase, and the surrounding argument is not Peter's, which is why this is an allusion and not a quotation. The formula recurs as the governing structure of 12:7-18, where the pattern “he shewed not himself … until after they had faith” is stated five times.

12:8.text: For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,

provenance.other: “heavenly gift” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The exact string “partakers of the heavenly gift” occurs in no KJV verse: Hebrews 6:4 reads “tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost”, so Moroni has fused the two halves of one verse, attaching Hebrews' participle to Hebrews' other noun.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:19 are fifteen verses apart and Ether 12:4 and 12:8 are four verses apart; the same page of Hebrews supplies the anchor of hope and the heavenly gift. Hebrews 6 is the chapter that warns it is impossible to renew apostates to repentance; Moroni takes its vocabulary and reverses its polarity, so that partaking of the heavenly gift is opened to “others” on the condition of faith rather than closed against them. What Hebrews uses to describe what is lost, Ether uses to describe what is available.

12:8.note: “He has shewn himself unto the world, and glorified the name of the Father, and prepared a way that thereby others might be partakers of the heavenly gift.” The distinctive noun phrase is a KJV singleton, and the participle Moroni attaches to it is the one Hebrews 6:4 uses two clauses later. The fusion is the evidence: an independent writer reaching for 'heavenly gift' would not also reach for 'partakers'. The 1830 “shewn” preserves the KJV spelling here as at 12:6, 12:7, 12:12, 12:21, 12:27, 12:28 and 12:31 — eight instances in one chapter, all modernized in 1920.

12:10.text: For by it the elders obtained a good report.

provenance.other: “the elders obtained” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “obtained a good report” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 11:2 and Hebrews 11:39, the opening and closing frames of the faith catalogue.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11 runs definition (11:1), then a summary claim about the ancients (11:2), then the catalogue (11:4-31). Ether 12 runs definition (12:6), then a summary claim about the ancients (12:10), then the catalogue (12:13-21). The order is what argues here, not the vocabulary: Moroni is not merely quoting Hebrews 11, he is reproducing its architecture, and 12:10 is the joint where that becomes checkable.

12:10.note: “It was by faith that they of old were called after the holy order of God.” Moroni's “they of old” answers Hebrews' “the elders”, and both sentences do the same structural job — a one-line claim that the ancients' standing came by faith, placed between the definition and the roll-call. The wording is not close enough for more than moderate: Moroni supplies a different predicate, the holy order, from the Book of Mormon's own Melchizedek material rather than from Hebrews 5 and 7. Recorded because the position in the argument is the evidence.

12:11.text: But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way.

provenance.other: “more excellent way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Hebrews 8:6 has “a more excellent ministry”, which is the nearest competitor and is not the phrase.
provenance.significance: This is the best metalepsis in the chapter. 1 Corinthians 12:31 is not a saying about excellence in general: it is the sentence with which Paul leaves the subject of spiritual gifts and introduces 1 Corinthians 13, so that in the King James Bible “a more excellent way” means, and can only mean, charity. Moroni writes it at 12:11 while discussing the law of Moses and the gift of the Son, and then his discourse arrives, seventeen verses later, exactly where Paul's does: at faith, hope and charity (12:28), at charity as the condition of inheritance (12:34), and at a prayer for charity (12:36). Moroni announces a more excellent way and then walks Paul's way. Whether the design is the writer's or the reader's, the phrase carries its destination with it.

12:11.note: “But in the gift of his Son, hath God prepared a more excellent way; and it is by faith that it hath been fulfilled.” The KJV has one more excellent way and it is Paul's introduction to the charity hymn. Two of the verse's other words are also in Moroni's neighbourhood — Paul's “gifts” beside Moroni's “gift of his Son”, Paul's “shew I unto you” beside Moroni's repeated “I will shew unto them” at 12:27-28. The phrase then reappears in Moroni's own mouth at 12:32 as “a more excellent hope”, which is a use no biblical verse licenses and which shows the phrase had become his.

12:13.text: And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:

provenance.other: There is little shared vocabulary and the link is not proposed on vocabulary. It is proposed on form: an anaphoric catalogue of exemplars, each introduced by the same faith-formula, running from named individuals to a rapid closing list.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11 names its worthies in pairs and clusters as the recitation accelerates — Gedeon and Barak, Samson and Jephthae, David and Samuel. Ether 12:13-15 does the same in the same place in the argument: Alma and Amulek, Nephi and Lehi, Ammon and his brethren. The Book of Mormon has written its own eleventh of Hebrews, with its own worthies substituted at every slot, and then, at 12:16, generalized in Hebrews' manner — “all they which wrought miracles, wrought them by faith” — before returning to a single extended exemplum, the brother of Jared, as Hebrews returns to none but instead to the sufferings of 11:35-38. The one place Moroni does not follow the model is the ending, and that is because his exemplum, unlike Hebrews', saw.

12:13.note: “Behold, it was the faith of Alma and Amulek that caused the prison to tumble to the earth.” The anaphora that runs 12:13, 12:14, 12:15, 12:17, 12:18, 12:19 and 12:20 is Hebrews 11's device — “By faith Abel … By faith Enoch … By faith Noah” — inflected into the Book of Mormon's own idiom, “Behold, it was the faith of X.” The catalogue is keyed here, at its first member, and the note covers the whole run rather than repeating at each verse. Note that the closest formal match is not the opening of Hebrews 11 but its summation at 11:32, where the names come in pairs and the writer says he has no more room; Moroni's equivalent is 12:16's “yea, and even all they which wrought miracles.”

12:14.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.other: “baptize you with the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 3:11, Mark 1:8 and Luke 3:16 — the same saying of John the Baptist in three Gospels. In all three the Holy Ghost is named before the fire; Ether 12:14 reverses the order.
provenance.alternative: The proximate model is not the KJV but the Book of Mormon's own earlier form of the phrase. 3 Nephi 9:20 reads “him will I baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost”, inverting the KJV's order of the two elements, and Ether 12:14 has the inverted order — “baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” The `mediation` enum has no value for an NT source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage; `OT-via-earlier-BoM` is the wrong shape because the source is not Old Testament. Recorded here as `uncertain` and flagged rather than resolved by inventing a value.
provenance.significance: The inversion is the finding. Every Gospel that has the saying has the Holy Ghost first and fire second (Matthew 3:11, Luke 3:16); the Book of Mormon consistently reverses it, and Ether 12:14 — a book presented as older than any of them, written last by Moroni — carries the reversed order. So the phrase reaches Ether not from the Bible directly but through a form the Book of Mormon has already standardized on.

12:14.note: “That they were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” Both nouns and the baptism verb are the KJV's, in an order no KJV verse has. The machine proposed Acts 13:52 (“filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost”) on the strength of five contiguous words; that is the wrong verse, because Acts 13:52 has no fire and no baptism. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is by this point a Book of Mormon formula, and formulae are poor evidence of a particular act of borrowing.

12:17.text: Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom.

provenance.other: “taste of death” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Matthew 16:28, Mark 9:1, Luke 9:27 and John 8:52. Three of the four are the same saying, and it is the saying about disciples standing here who will not taste of death.
provenance.alternative: The proximate model is again an earlier Book of Mormon passage rather than the Bible: 3 Nephi 28:7 grants the three disciples that they “shall never taste of death”, and Ether 12:17 refers back to that grant explicitly (“the three disciples obtained a promise”). As at 12:14 the enum has no value for an NT source arriving through an earlier Book of Mormon text; recorded `uncertain` and explained rather than forced.
provenance.significance: The KJV's not-tasting-death saying is spoken to disciples standing in front of Jesus and is left, in all three Synoptics, unexplained — the interpretive crux of the passage is what it means that some of them did not die. The Book of Mormon answers it: three disciples, in another hemisphere, who did not. Moroni's contribution here is to make faith the mechanism (“they obtained not the promise until after their faith”), which neither the Gospels nor 3 Nephi 28 says.

12:17.note: “It was by faith that the three disciples obtained a promise that they should not taste of death.” The idiom is the KJV's and the situation is the KJV saying's, transposed. Note the second half of the verse, “they obtained not the promise until after their faith”, which is Hebrews 11:39's clause — “these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise” — with the negation moved: Hebrews' worthies did not receive it, Moroni's did, once their faith was in place. Two verses of Hebrews 11 (33's “obtained promises”, 39's “received not the promise”) sit under one sentence.

12:17.text: And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise:

provenance.other: “obtained promises” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:33; “obtained a good report” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 11:2 and 11:39. Moroni's sentence has both halves of the collocation — obtained a promise, and did not obtain it until faith — and the verb is Hebrews' throughout.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:39 is the closing sentence of the faith catalogue and its point is deferral: the worthies obtained a report but not the promise, because God provided some better thing for us. Moroni's catalogue closes the same way and reverses the verdict — his exemplars do obtain, and what stands between them and the obtaining is only the interval before faith. The chapter's whole polemic against not-seeing is aimed at that interval.

12:17.note: “And they obtained not the promise until after their faith.” The clause is Hebrews 11:39's, minus the deferral. Moderate rather than high because 'obtain the promise' is not by itself distinctive English and the case rests on the position in a catalogue that is already Hebrews 11's.

12:19.text: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;

provenance.other: “within the veil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Hebrews 10:20 has “through the veil”, Exodus and Leviticus have “within the vail” of the tabernacle in a different spelling that `kjv-rarity` does not conflate; the phrase as spelled here belongs to Hebrews 6:19 alone.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 6:19's veil is entered by hope; Ether 12:19's is a barrier that strong faith cannot be kept outside of, and 12:21's is one the brother of Jared can no longer be kept without. The Book of Mormon has taken a metaphor of access and made it a threshold in a narrative — the veil is now a thing a man stands on one side of and then does not. This is where the anchor of 12:4 arrives, and the two verses should be read together.

12:19.note: “Many whose faith was so exceeding strong even before Christ came, which could not be kept from within the veil.” The phrase is a KJV singleton and its verse is the one already standing behind 12:4, which makes recurrence rather than volume the argument: one verse of Hebrews supplies the opening image of the discourse and the pivot of its climax. Note the 1830 relative “which” for persons, corrected to “who” in 1920 — the KJV's own usage, and one more sign of the register the chapter is composed in.

12:19.text: Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.

provenance.other: “and was glad” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Esther 8:15, Psalm 97:8 and John 8:56 — and only John 8:56 predicates it of a man before Christ who saw Christ. The sequence saw-it-and-was-glad is that verse's.
provenance.significance: John 8:56 is the New Testament's own statement of the problem Ether 12:19 exists to solve: how a believer who lived before Christ nevertheless saw him. Jesus asserts it of Abraham without explaining it; Moroni generalizes it to a class — 'many whose faith was so exceeding strong even before Christ came' — and supplies the mechanism, the eye of faith becoming sight. Read the two together and Moroni is answering the Jews' objection in John 8:57, that a man not yet fifty years old cannot have been seen by Abraham.

12:19.note: “But truly saw with their eyes the things which they had beheld with an eye of faith, and they were glad.” The clause closes on John 8:56's three words in John 8:56's order, and the whole verse is about the one thing John 8:56 claims: pre-Christian sight of Christ, ending in gladness. The middle of the verse belongs to Hebrews 11:13 — “having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them” — so the sentence looks through Hebrews' distant sight to John's actual seeing. Moderate because “and they were glad” is short and the shared vocabulary with John is thin; what raises it above an echo is that the subject matter is identical and rare.

12:23.text: And Moses said unto the LORD, O my LORD, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.

provenance.other: There is almost no shared wording and the link is not offered on wording; “am not eloquent” is a KJV singleton but Moroni does not use it. The case is the scene.
provenance.significance: The commissioning objection is a fixed Old Testament form: the prophet protests his inadequacy of utterance, and God answers by asserting who made the mouth. Moroni runs it with one substitution that is the whole point — the medium is writing rather than speech. “Thou hast made us mighty in word by faith, whereunto thou hast not made us mighty in writing”; “thou hast made us that we could write but little, because of the awkwardness of our hands.” The Lord's reply at 12:26-27 is the Exodus 4:11-12 reply in Pauline vocabulary: not I will be with thy mouth, but my grace is sufficient and weakness is given on purpose. A book that presents itself as a written record has taken scripture's standing scene about speech and converted it into a scene about the hand.

12:23.note: Recorded as figural and flagged as such: the wording will not bear more, and CONVENTIONS §5's Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry is the warning against pressing typology past the words. What justifies a link rather than an exclusion is that Moroni's objection is not a general complaint but the specific commissioning-objection form, made in the second person to God, answered by God in the next sentence, and answered with a statement about how God makes people — which is Exodus 4:11's “who hath made man's mouth?” The Jeremiah 1:6 objection (“I cannot speak: for I am a child”) is the same form and would serve equally; Exodus 4:10 is named because it is the fullest.
12:23.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared. A reader who requires verbal contact should decline this link; it is proposed on the shape of the scene and on the fact that the divine answer at 12:27 addresses the objection in the terms Exodus 4:11 does.

12:26.text: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

provenance.other: “my grace is sufficient” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The frame is reproduced with it: Paul writes “And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee”, Moroni writes “the Lord spake unto me, saying … my grace is sufficient for the meek.” Both are first-person reports of a divine answer to a complaint about weakness, and in both the answer is that same sentence.
provenance.significance: The borrowing is not of a phrase but of an entire rhetorical situation, and the situation is 2 Corinthians 12's: an apostle boasting reluctantly, conscious of a weakness he has asked to have removed, receiving in reply a refusal that is also a promise. Moroni's weakness is his prose; Paul's is unspecified. What Moroni adds is a change of addressee — Paul's “for thee” becomes “for the meek”, then at 12:27 “for all men that humble themselves before me” — turning a private oracle into a general law, which is exactly what the chapter has been doing to Hebrews 11:1 since 12:6.

12:26.note: “Fools mock, but they shall mourn; and my grace is sufficient for the meek, that they shall take no advantage of your weakness.” The KJV's one grace-is-sufficient verse, reported in the same words and in the same frame — a divine answer, quoted, to a complaint about weakness. This is one of the least deniable New Testament borrowings in the Book of Mormon, and the chapter goes on to build its distinctive weak-things-made-strong doctrine out of the rest of the verse at 12:27. The machine also proposed Ezekiel 39:10 for “they shall take no”; see the exclusion register.

12:26.text: Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous there is favour.

provenance.other: “make a mock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The collocation of fools with mocking as their characteristic act is otherwise Proverbs 1:22-26's, where Wisdom promises to laugh at the calamity of the scorners.
provenance.significance: Moroni has been afraid of mockery for three verses — “the Gentiles will mock at these things”, “I fear lest the Gentiles shall mock at our words.” The Lord's answer opens with a proverb-shaped antithesis of exactly the KJV's kind: fools mock, but they shall mourn. The reversal of laughter into mourning is the sapiential move of Proverbs 1:26 and of James 4:9; naming Proverbs 14:9 is naming the KJV's only verse that makes mocking the defining act of fools.

12:26.note: “Fools mock, but they shall mourn.” Four words, in the antithetical form the King James Proverbs uses constantly, with the KJV's one fools-and-mocking verse behind them. Moderate: 'fool' and 'mock' are common words and the sentence could be composed without a source. It is recorded because it stands at the head of a divine reply and because it is the one clause in the chapter whose register is Wisdom rather than Paul.

12:27.text: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;

provenance.other: “weak things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “confound the wise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon's most quoted single sentence about weakness therefore rests on a phrase found nowhere else in the King James Bible.
provenance.significance: Recover 1 Corinthians 1 and the fit is closer than the phrase alone suggests. Paul's argument is that the preaching of the cross is foolishness to them that perish, that the Greeks seek after wisdom and count it folly, and that God chose the foolish and weak things of the world to shame the wise and mighty. Moroni's situation, four verses earlier, is that “the Gentiles will mock at these things, because of our weakness in writing.” The Gentiles who mock a weak text are Paul's Greeks; the answer given to Moroni is Paul's answer, that the weak thing is chosen on purpose. And it is chosen, in Paul, to confound precisely those who mock. Moroni's oracle does not say this. 1 Corinthians 1:27 says it for him.

12:27.note: “I give unto men weakness, that they may be humble … then will I make weak things become strong unto them.” The two-word phrase is a KJV singleton and the doctrine built on it is the chapter's most famous sentence. Note what Moroni changes: Paul's weak things are chosen to confound the mighty and remain weak; Moroni's are made strong. The change is doctrinally substantial and verbally minimal, which is the signature of a borrowing rather than a coincidence — an independent writer reaching for this idea in English would be very unlikely to reach for these two words.

12:27.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

provenance.other: “out of weakness were made strong” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is inside the faith catalogue Ether 12 has been reciting since 12:13.
provenance.significance: This is the finding that makes the second half of the chapter cohere with the first. Moroni's weak-things-made-strong doctrine is usually read as a development of 2 Corinthians 12:9, and it is; but the actual proposition — that weakness is turned into strength — is stated in the King James Bible in exactly one place, and that place is Hebrews 11, four verses after the catalogue Moroni has just finished imitating. So the oracle at 12:27 is not a departure from the chapter's Hebrews 11 programme; it is the programme's next line. Moroni recites Hebrews 11's worthies at 12:13-21, and Hebrews 11's own summary of what faith did for them — out of weakness were made strong — becomes the promise made to him at 12:27 and kept to him at 12:37, “because thou hast seen thy weakness, thou shalt be made strong.”
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 is the other candidate and is certainly also present in the passage (see the link at 12:26). The two are not alternatives so much as a fusion: Paul supplies the grace-is-sufficient frame and the vocabulary of glorying in weakness; Hebrews 11:34 supplies the actual weak-to-strong transformation, which Paul does not state — his strength is made perfect in weakness, which is not the same claim.

12:27.note: “Then will I make weak things become strong unto them”, and at 12:37, “because thou hast seen thy weakness, thou shalt be made strong.” The KJV's only weakness-to-strength clause is Hebrews 11:34's, and Moroni uses the transformation twice, ten verses apart, in a discourse otherwise built on Hebrews 11 from end to end. Below any quotation threshold on length; the argument is rarity plus the chapter's established dependence on the source's immediate context.

12:27.text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.

provenance.other: “humble themselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni has it twice in one sentence — “all men that humble themselves before me: for if they humble themselves before me” — and the sentence, like 2 Chronicles 7:14, is a conditional promise in the divine first person.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 7:14 is the KJV's classic if-then oracle: if my people humble themselves, then will I hear. Ether 12:27 has the same grammar with different conditions and a different apodosis — if they humble themselves and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong. The Old Testament formula supplies the syntax into which the Pauline and Hebraic material of the verse is poured, which is worth noticing: the doctrine is New Testament, the sentence-shape is Chronicles.

12:27.note: “My grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me: for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.” A KJV singleton verb-phrase, doubled, inside a then-will-I conditional. Moderate rather than high because 'humble themselves' is unremarkable English and the doubling may be Moroni's own emphasis rather than an echo; recorded because the conditional structure matches as well as the phrase.

12:28.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

provenance.other: “faith, hope, charity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni's “faith, hope, and charity” inserts the conjunction; the triad and its order are the KJV's, and 'charity' rather than 'love' is the King James translators' choice at this verse and not the choice of most English versions before or since.
provenance.significance: The triad is the culmination of a discourse that has run through faith (12:3-22) and hope (12:4, 12:9, 12:32) in order, and it arrives with the third term unannounced. That is Paul's shape too: 1 Corinthians 13 is introduced by 12:31's 'more excellent way' — the phrase Moroni used at 12:11 — and ends on the triad. Moroni's discourse enters Paul's chapter at its door and leaves by its window. The word charity is then repeated at 12:34, 12:35, 12:36 and 12:37, so a chapter that began by defining faith ends by making charity the condition of inheritance, which is 1 Corinthians 13:2's judgment exactly.

12:28.note: “I will shew unto them that faith, hope, and charity, bringeth unto me the fountain of all righteousness.” The KJV's one occurrence of the triad, in its order, with the King James word for the third term. What Moroni adds is a destination — the triad brings men to God — where Paul only ranks the three. The 1830 “shew”, modernized in 1920, is the KJV's spelling; the machine proposed Daniel 2:24 for “I will shew unto the” and that is a formula, not a source (see the exclusion register).

12:30.text: And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you.

provenance.other: “remove hence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 17:20; “remove mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:2. Moroni's construction — a man speaking to a named mountain, the imperative 'Remove', and the mountain removing — is Matthew 17:20's alone; Mark 11:23 has 'Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea', a different imperative.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is worth stating plainly. In the King James Bible, faith that removes mountains occurs twice: once as Jesus' promise (Matthew 17:20) and once as Paul's example of a faith that is worthless without charity (1 Corinthians 13:2, “though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing”). Ether 12 cites the mountain at 12:30 and arrives at charity at 12:34, where the verdict is that without charity men “cannot inherit that place.” Moroni has, without quoting Paul, reproduced Paul's sequence and Paul's judgment on it. Whoever composed the chapter had 1 Corinthians 13 in view — 12:11 and 12:28 prove that independently — and the mountain of 12:30 is the example that chapter itself uses.

12:30.note: “The brother of Jared said unto the mountain Zerin, Remove, and it was removed.” The bare imperative to a mountain, and the mountain's obedience, is Matthew 17:20's sentence with the mountain named. That the Book of Mormon supplies a proper name where the Gospel says 'this mountain' is characteristic: the promise is turned into an event, as the not-tasting-death saying was at 12:17 and as John 8:56's Abraham was at 12:19. Three times in this chapter an unexplained New Testament claim is given a narrative that discharges it.

12:32.text: In my Father’s house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.

provenance.other: “mansions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “prepare a place” occurs in exactly two, John 14:2 and 14:3, consecutive verses of the same saying. Ether 12:32 has both — a prepared house, among the mansions of the Father — and so has all of John 14:2's distinctive vocabulary in one sentence.
provenance.significance: The King James translators' 'mansions' for μοναί is a choice no modern version keeps (rooms, dwelling places), so a text depending on the word depends on the KJV and on nothing earlier or later. What Moroni does with it is to make it the terminus of the hope he defined at 12:4: hope is an anchor, hope is for a better world, and here at last the better world is named, and named in John's words. The verse also completes 12:11's phrase — “a more excellent way” has become “a more excellent hope” — so the two Pauline and Johannine strands of the chapter meet in one sentence.

12:32.note: “Thou hast prepared a house for man; yea, even among the mansions of thy Father, in the which man might have a more excellent hope; wherefore man must hope, or he cannot receive an inheritance in the place which thou hast prepared.” House, mansions, Father, prepared, place — the whole content of John 14:2, redistributed. Hardy's apparatus cross-references John 14:2 here and the reference is exactly right. The 1830 reads “in the which”, a KJV relative construction the 1920 edition simplified to “which”, and the same formula appears at Enos 1:27 (“a place prepared for you in the mansions of my Father”), so the phrase is one the Book of Mormon has used before; the recurrence strengthens rather than weakens the case, since the source of both is the same singleton.

12:33.text: Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.

provenance.other: “take it again” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:17 and John 10:18 — the same saying, twice. “lay down my life” occurs in exactly three, John 10:15, 10:17 and 13:37. Moroni's clause “even unto the laying down of thy life for the world, that thou mightest take it again” has both halves of John 10:17 in John 10:17's order.
provenance.significance: The laying down and taking again is a Johannine formula with no Synoptic parallel, and Moroni reproduces the causal structure as well as the words: in John the Father loves the Son BECAUSE he lays down his life to take it again; in Ether the Son's love of the world is expressed AS the laying down of his life to take it again. The direction of the love has moved from Father-to-Son to Son-to-world, which is John 3:16's direction. So one sentence holds John 10's formula inside John 3:16's proposition and ends in John 14:2's prepared place — three Johannine sayings in a row, in the order a reader of John would meet them.

12:33.note: “Thou hast loved the world, even unto the laying down of thy life for the world, that thou mightest take it again to prepare a place for the children of men.” Hardy cross-references John 10:17-18 at this verse and the wording bears it out precisely. The final clause returns to John 14:2's “prepare a place”, which is why 12:32 and 12:33 have to be read as one movement; and the purpose Moroni assigns to the resurrection — that Christ took his life again in order to prepare a place — is a joining of the two Johannine sayings that neither text makes.

12:33.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

provenance.other: “so loved the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni does not have the intensifier — he writes “thou hast loved the world” — which is why this is moderate rather than high; loved-the-world without 'so' is not a KJV string.
provenance.significance: John 3:16's proposition is that God's love of the world took the form of a gift, and the gift is the Son. Ether 12:33 makes the same proposition with the Son as the subject rather than the object, and specifies the gift as his own life. Held next to the John 10 borrowing in the same verse, the effect is that the Book of Mormon has said what John 3:16 says using John 10:17's vocabulary — which is not what either verse says on its own, and is the reason 12:34 can then identify that love as charity.

12:33.note: “That thou hast loved the world.” The clause is short and the argument is contextual: this is the only KJV proposition about God loving the world, it is the best-known verse in the English Bible, and Moroni immediately draws from it the conclusion that this love “is charity” (12:34). Recorded as moderate because the intensifier is absent and 'love the world' has a different and opposed sense at 1 John 2:15, which the exclusion register notes.

12:34.text: And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.

provenance.other: “remove mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is this one; the mountain of Ether 12:30 stands four verses earlier. The conditional 'have not charity, therefore nothing' is 1 Corinthians 13:1-3's refrain, stated three times there and once here.
provenance.significance: Paul's argument is that the greatest exercises of faith are void without charity. Moroni's chapter has spent thirty verses arguing that faith moves prison walls, changes Lamanites, opens the veil and removes mountains — the exact list Paul discounts — and then concludes that without charity none of it secures the inheritance. Read as a whole, Ether 12 is a defence of faith that ends by subordinating faith to charity, which is the structure of 1 Corinthians 12:31-13:13 and of nothing else in scripture.

12:34.note: “Except men shall have charity, they cannot inherit that place which thou hast prepared in the mansions of thy Father.” The condition is Paul's, with an inheritance substituted for Paul's 'I am nothing'. Confidence is high on the strength of the chapter's other two demonstrable contacts with the same Pauline unit — 12:11's KJV-singleton 'more excellent way', which is 1 Corinthians 12:31, and 12:28's KJV-singleton triad, which is 13:13 — so this verse is not being read into Paul from a distance; it sits between two verses that are certainly his.

12:35.text: Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents.

provenance.other: “take therefore the talent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “unto every one that hath shall be given” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:29. Moroni's “take away their talent, yea, even that which they have received, and give unto them which shall have more abundantly” has the talent and the transfer of Matthew 25:28 and the that-which-they-have of 25:29.
provenance.alternative: Moroni's closing phrase is “more abundantly”, and Matthew 25:29 reads “he shall have abundance” while the parallel logion at Matthew 13:12 reads “he shall have more abundance” — a KJV singleton. `mediation-check.py` on Ether 12:35 against Matthew 25:29 and Matthew 13:12 finds no decisive divergence, because Moroni reproduces neither verse's surrounding clause; so the comparative cannot be pressed. It is recorded because Hardy's cross-reference is to Matthew 25 alone, and the one word Moroni adds beyond Matthew 25's wording happens to be the word Matthew 13:12 has.
provenance.significance: The parable of the talents is a story about a servant judged for what he did with what he received; Moroni applies it to the Gentiles who receive his record. That is a substantial reassignment — the talent is now a book, the servant is now a readership, and the condition of forfeiture is charity rather than industry. Note that the parable then supplies the chapter's own conclusion two verses later: 'thou hast been faithful' at 12:37 is the lord's commendation at Matthew 25:21, so the same parable both threatens the Gentiles and acquits Moroni.

12:35.note: “That thou wilt prove them, and take away their talent, yea, even that which they have received, and give unto them which shall have more abundantly.” Hardy cross-references Matthew 25:28-29 here; the wording supports it, with 'talent' as the decisive term — it is a unit of weight nowhere else in the Book of Mormon and its only KJV life as a thing given and taken away is this parable. The 1830 relative 'which' for persons is again the KJV's usage, corrected in 1920.

12:37.text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

provenance.other: “thou hast been faithful” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 25:21, Matthew 25:23 and Luke 19:17. Two of the three are the parable of the talents, whose other end Moroni has just quoted at 12:35; the third is its Lucan cousin.
provenance.significance: This is our own addition to Hardy's row, and it is what makes his row larger than it looks. Hardy cross-references Matthew 25:28-29 at 12:35, the parable's judgment on the unprofitable servant. Two verses later Moroni receives the parable's blessing on the profitable one, in the parable's own words, from the Lord speaking directly to him: 'thou hast been faithful.' The whole of the chapter's ending is therefore staged inside Matthew 25 — the Gentiles in the place of the servant who buried the talent, Moroni in the place of the servant commended — and the reward Matthew promises, 'enter thou into the joy of thy lord', becomes 'the sitting down in the place which I have prepared in the mansions of my Father.' Neither Hardy's apparatus nor the verse itself says this; the pair of quotations says it.

12:37.note: “If they have not charity, it mattereth not unto thee, thou hast been faithful.” Four words shared with a parable already demonstrably in view two verses earlier, spoken in the same voice (a lord commending a servant) and to the same effect (the servant is admitted where the other is dispossessed). What raises this above coincidence is the pairing: a chapter that quotes Matthew 25:28 and then Matthew 25:21 has read the parable, not remembered a phrase from it.

12:37.text: Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way, and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared.

provenance.other: “the place which I have prepared” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ether 12:37 has it word for word, in the divine first person, as Exodus does.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 23:20 has a New Testament quotation — Matthew 11:10, Mark 1:2 and Luke 7:27 all cite 'Behold, I send my messenger before thy face' — so the mediation question is real. `mediation-check.py` on Ether 12:37 against Exodus 23:20 and Matthew 11:10 returns one decisive point: the entire clause Moroni reproduces, 'to bring thee into the place which I have prepared', is absent from the Gospel form, which stops at the messenger and replaces the destination with 'shall prepare thy way before thee'. The Book of Mormon has the Old Testament form. Mediation is `direct-OT` on that evidence.
provenance.significance: The prepared place of Ether 12:32-37 has been Johannine for five verses — the mansions of the Father — and here, in the one clause where it is God who has prepared and God who is speaking, the words are Exodus'. Exodus 23:20's prepared place is Canaan and the promise is escorted arrival; Moroni's is heaven and the escort is his own faithfulness. That the two frames are welded without seam is characteristic of the chapter, which does the same thing at 12:4 with Hebrews and Corinthians.

12:37.note: “Even unto the sitting down in the place which I have prepared in the mansions of my Father.” Seven words identical to a KJV singleton, inside a sentence whose other half is John 14:2's. Moderate rather than high because the component words are all common and the string could in principle be assembled independently from 'prepare a place' in John 14:2 — which is why the mediation check matters: the exact string, with 'which I have', exists in the KJV once, and Moroni has it.

12:38.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, and nowhere else; the KJV's other judgment seats belong to Pilate, Gallio and Herod. The 1830 spells it 'judgement seat' and the 1920 hyphenates, 'judgment-seat'.
provenance.alternative: The phrase is by Moroni's point in the record a Book of Mormon formula (Jacob 6:13, 2 Nephi 33:11, Moroni 10:34 all use it in the same farewell posture), so the proximate model may be the Book of Mormon's own earlier farewells rather than Paul. The enum has no value for an NT source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage; the link is recorded `direct-NT` because Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10 are the only English source the formula can have, and the route through the earlier farewells is stated here rather than encoded.
provenance.significance: Both Pauline verses put the judgment seat at the end of an argument about how Christians treat one another — Romans 14 about not judging a brother, 2 Corinthians 5 about persuading men. Moroni's farewell is doing both: he has just been told that the Gentiles' failure of charity is not chargeable to him, and he takes leave of the Gentiles and of his brethren in one sentence. The tribunal is invoked as the place where the reckoning he has been relieved of will nevertheless be made.

12:38.note: “Until we shall meet before the judgement seat of Christ, where all men shall know that my garments are not spotted with your blood.” Four words shared with a phrase the KJV uses twice, in the posture Paul uses it in. The 1830 spelling 'judgement' is the older form and was regularized in 1920; it is orthographic rather than substantive, but it belongs in the record under CONVENTIONS §8.

12:38.text: Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.

provenance.other: “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The garment half of Moroni's image is Jude 1:23's, “the garment spotted by the flesh” — the KJV's only spotted garment outside Jacob's flocks in Genesis 30, where 'spotted' means piebald cattle and has nothing to do with defilement.
provenance.significance: Moroni's sentence fuses two verses that the Bible keeps apart: Paul's declaration of innocence of his hearers' blood (Acts 20:26, spoken as a farewell at Miletus, exactly the situation here) and Jude's spotted garment. Neither has both terms. The Book of Mormon does this fusion repeatedly — Jacob 1:19 and 2 Nephi 9:44 both shake the garments clean of blood — so the compound is by Moroni an inherited idiom, and this verse is its last use in the book.
provenance.alternative: As at 12:38's judgment seat, the proximate model is likely the Book of Mormon's own earlier formula rather than the KJV; `direct-NT` records the ultimate English source, and the intermediate route is stated here because the enum has no value for it.

12:38.note: “Where all men shall know that my garments are not spotted with your blood.” The declaration of blood-innocence at a farewell is Acts 20:26's and the spotted garment is Jude 1:23's, and the sentence needs both. Moderate: no long verbal run, and the compound is a Book of Mormon formula by this point, which makes it evidence of the book's habits rather than of a fresh act of borrowing at this verse.

12:39.text: And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. And he turned again into the camp: but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle.

provenance.other: “face to face” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses and is not by itself distinctive. What is distinctive is the two-part construction: face to face, followed immediately by an as-a-man simile. “as a man speaketh unto his friend” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Exodus 33:11 is therefore the only KJV verse that has both halves — 'face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend' — and Ether 12:39 has 'face to face, and that he told me in plain humility, even as a man telleth another in mine own language.' The machine's proposal of Numbers 14:14 catches the common phrase and misses the construction; see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: Exodus 33:11 is the KJV's charter text for the highest grade of prophetic access, and Deuteronomy 34:10 makes it the criterion by which no prophet since has equalled Moses. Moroni claims it, in Moses' own construction, in the last words of his book — and then adds a clause Moses does not have, 'in mine own language', which converts the simile into a claim about translation and about the very inadequacy of writing he complained of at 12:23-25. The chapter that began by protesting the awkwardness of Moroni's hands ends with the Lord speaking to him as a man speaks to his friend, in his own language.

12:39.note: “He hath talked with me face to face, and that he told me in plain humility, even as a man telleth another in mine own language.” The KJV's face-to-face-plus-simile construction occurs once, at Exodus 33:11, and Moroni reproduces both halves with his own substitutions in the simile (telleth another for speaketh unto his friend). Deuteronomy 34:10, 'whom the LORD knew face to face', is the verse that makes the claim exclusive to Moses and is worth reading beside it. High rather than certain because the individual phrase is common; the construction is what carries it.

12:39.text: Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? are not ye my work in the Lord?

provenance.other: “seen Jesus” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Elsewhere the KJV writes 'seen the Lord' (John 20:18, 20:25, 1 Corinthians 9:1 aside) or names him otherwise; the bare collocation is Paul's here alone.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 9:1 is Paul authenticating his apostleship against people who dispute it, and the ground he offers is that he has seen Jesus. Moroni, having spent the chapter fearing that the Gentiles will mock his writing, offers the same credential in the same words and to the same end: 'then shall ye know that I have seen Jesus.' Given that the chapter demonstrably has 1 Corinthians 1, 12 and 13 in view, the Corinthian correspondence's own self-defence formula appearing at the point where Moroni defends himself is at least worth recording.

12:39.note: “And then shall ye know that I have seen Jesus.” Three words, one of them the KJV's only 'seen Jesus'. Filed as an echo, not an allusion: the phrase is short, the situation supplies most of the case, and a writer could reach these words without a source. Recorded because the chapter's Pauline density makes the coincidence worth a reader's attention rather than silence.

12:41.text: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.

provenance.other: “three that bear record” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ether 12:41 names the same three in the same order — the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ (for 'the Word'), and the Holy Ghost — and attaches to the third of them the same verb, 'which beareth record'.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest `kjvSpecific` claim in the chapter, and it is strong for a reason that has nothing to do with rarity counts. 1 John 5:7 as printed here is the Johannine Comma: it is absent from every Greek manuscript before the sixteenth century, absent from the Vulgate's oldest witnesses, and present in the King James Bible because Erasmus admitted it under pressure into his third edition. A text dependent on this verse cannot be dependent on any Greek New Testament; it can only be dependent on the Latin-and-Erasmus tradition that the KJV transmits. Availability, in Hays's sense, does not merely fail on the Book of Mormon's own chronology here — it fails on the text-critical history of the source itself.
provenance.alternative: The triadic form is also the shape of 2 Corinthians 13:14's benediction and of Matthew 28:19's baptismal formula, both of which are ordinary KJV text; if the resemblance is to a generic trinitarian triad rather than to this verse, the argument above does not apply. What weighs against the generic reading is the verb: Matthew and 2 Corinthians have no bearing of record, and 1 John 5:7 is the only KJV verse in which the three are said to bear record.

12:41.note: “That the Grace of God the Father, and also the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost, which beareth record of them, may be, and abide in you forever. Amen.” The three persons, in order, with 'bear record' predicated of the Holy Ghost — 1 John 5:7's content in a benediction's grammar. The benediction's own frame is 2 Corinthians 13:14's, 'the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen', including the closing Amen; the two are fused, as Hebrews and Corinthians were fused at 12:4 and John 10 and John 3 at 12:33. That the last sentence of Moroni's discourse should rest on the KJV's most famous interpolated verse is a fact the catalogue should state plainly rather than leave to a footnote.

12:41.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.

provenance.other: The KJV's apostolic benedictions are numerous but only 2 Corinthians 13:14 names all three persons, begins with grace, and ends 'Amen'. “abide in you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 15:7 and 1 John 2:24, which supply Moroni's closing verb.
provenance.significance: Moroni ends his farewell with the form in which the Pauline letters end, which is consistent with a chapter that has been reading 1 and 2 Corinthians since 12:11. The one alteration is that Paul's benediction wishes the three to be WITH the reader and Moroni's wishes them to ABIDE IN him — a Johannine verb, from the discourse the chapter has already drawn on at 14:2. The last sentence of Ether 12 is therefore a Pauline benediction with Johannine content, which is a fair description of the whole discourse.

12:41.note: “May be, and abide in you forever. Amen.” The tripartite grace-benediction with its closing Amen. Moderate: benedictions are formulaic by nature and the individual words are unremarkable, so the case rests on the completeness of the match — three persons, grace first, Amen last — rather than on any rare string.
